HERITAGE WARS

By: Julie Laurenz | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Dodgy developers are buying up protected heritage buildings in Durban, allowing them to rot, then slap parking lots and high-rises in their place. City planning seems complicit.

Summary:
Architectural activists say dodgy developers are buying up protected heritage buildings in Durban, and allowing them to rot so that they can slap parking lots and high-rises in their place, changing the face of some of the city’s most historical suburbs. They alleged that city planning is helping them do it. And from the evidence this certainly seems to be the case.

VISUAL TREATMENT:
Seems it’s a story dealing with architecture I think it would be visually relevant to shoot interviews, links etc in “architectural settings” relevant to the subject matter. So if we are speaking to Prof Professor Brian Kearney about DBN being regarded as one of the most significant repositories of Art Deco – we could look at including an angle during the interview that would look skyward from the feet to show such a building towering behind.
I have spoken to cameraman Ryan Logie (he has just bought a camera similar to the one Ian Millar used in CT to shoot the foetal surgery story – you like the images) He has a set of portable tracks we can make use off. We’ll also get some good time lapses of some of the art deco/Edwardian and Victorian buildings in Durban. These “grand design” shots will be contrasted with the derelict shots of the heritage buildings that have been left to rot and the massive concrete blocks of apartments/parking lots.



Further information:
THE STORY
• THE PINK HOUSE
MAIN CHARACTER: Cheryl Johnson. Very articulate and passionate. A features writer for magazines.
The Save our Berea is a group of architects and residents who have come together, specifically to protest against eThekwini's lack of by-law enforcement and serial neglect of a historically important buildings on Durban’s Berea.
The organisation was started by Cheryl Johnson 18months ago (Her husband is a well known Durban architect) when a 100 year old tin and iron home on Essenwood Rd– known to Durbanites as “The Pink House” – was unceremoniously flattened and an a parking garage type began to be built. The home had belonged to an old lady who had passed away. (We have photos of the house before from the family)
It is illegal in Durban to alter or demolish listed buildings more than 60-years-old, without approval procedures, including the need to advertise in the KZN Government Gazette and to allow for a new 30-day period for objections. The “Pink House” should have been protected building.
Cheryl began investigating and discovered that AMAFA had given the new owners permission to demolish because the home had been set ablaze and virtually destroyed. If heritage buildings are deemed unsafe AMAFA will allow it to be pulled down. And here is where things start to go awry. According to the fire department it was an act of arson. They opened a case but unfortunately they couldn’t pinpoint who had set the fire. (Have copy of docket/they found an accelerant)
Suspicious, she began to dig deeper. When the city refused to hand over information regarding the planning and building of the new parking lot she used PAIA and uncovered all kinds of discrepancies.
• The original plans were submitted by un unregistered architect (illegal)
• That the plans submitted to the city and AMAFA are different plans.
• The plans submitted to AMAFA have a forged signature of another (registered) architect on them.
• Apparently it’s possible to stand outside the building with the plans and point out 137 discrepancies between what’s being built and the plans at the city.
Cheryl says this investigation opened a can of worms across the Berea. She started a website called “Save Our Berea” within days she had 40 000 members and at their first meeting over 400 people arrived.
Here are some of the other cases:
• 317 CURRIE ROAD
MAIN CHARACTER: Advocate T Abubaker. Also articulate and passionate.
CURRENT: This court battle starts today.

Currie Road in Durban has major historical significance in Durban. Virtually every home on the road is a protected building. Many of the city’s first Indian merchants who came to trade in the 1900’s built homes along this road. They were forcibly removed later.
Now there is a battle looming over a high-rise development that has been slapped adjacent on top of and adjacent to some classic Victorian styled homes.
Despite the cities own plan for the area that says the properties should remain Gr1 – residential, the developers at 317 Currier Rd managed to get the city to rezone just this plot to a Gr5 - commercial, high-density, high-rise buildings.
Other Concerns:
• The plans originally said a 3 storey building – now it’s up to 9 floors.
• The building is devaluating the properties next to it (not allowed according to building and city planning by laws – I have the legislation)
• The homes around it are cast in shadow for a large portion of the day (though we could so a nice time delay)
• But the residents accuse the municipality of flouting bylaws by allowing the development. The law simply states that intentions to rezone property should be advertised to everyone within 100 metres of the said property, but many say they weren’t informed. (I have a group who can confirm this)
Advocate Abubaker is fuming. There is literally no more than a few inches of space between his balcony and the wall of the high-rise. He is leading the charge against the developers and the city.
Other related cases:
1. Cadogan Gardens resident Hardy Wilson said he was aware of the development when he bought his flat in December 2012. “I went to the municipality to inquire about the development and they showed me approved plans for a four-storey building. The amended plans were only approved this year.”
2. One of the most affected buildings is 6 Winter Gardens, which has units valued at more than R6 million. The new development stands directly in front of it. Alan Ross, who lives next to the development, said he had received the notice for the rezoning application, but he said it was incorrectly phrased and most of the details had been omitted. Ross is concerned about his privacy and said occupants of the new building would have an unobstructed view into parts of his home.
The residents said they had made numerous trips to the municipal offices, but had been denied access to building plans, officials citing “copyright reasons”.
WHAT THE CITY / DEVELOPERS HAVE TO SAY
eThekwini spokeswoman Tozi Mthethwa said due process had been followed and all the affected neighbours were correctly notified. She said that the municipality is unaware of any irregularities in the process and, if there were any, the affected parties should have brought the complaint to the municipality’s attention at that point, not three years later.
The developer, Serengeti Rise Industries (Pty) Ltd, lawyer Richard Hoal, says that the company is constructing in accordance with an approved building plan and other approvals granted by the eThekwini Municipality. He say anything about the changing of plans from four storeys to nine storeys.
• POYNTON ROAD
It seems that even when people do object to a development their complaints are ignored. Another parking lot type development has been pushed through the city council despite 47 listed objections by residents.
The main fellow is Wayne Webb, he is a carpenter, BUT with 4 degrees including a masters in math. He’s a bit of a hippy type, but super smart and passionate. I don’t want to clutter the story with people – so I may just get Cheryl to run through this point with us.
• THE TROJAN HOUSES
There are a whole bunch of beautiful homes on the Berea that are being left to rot by developers in the hopes that AMAFA will grant them demolition orders. I suggest we talk to one who has at least 2 different properties: Yunus Motalla. He’s a millionaire and can certainly afford to fix up these properties. He is the one with plans (although unconfirmed yet) to build a bottle store on top of one of the most beautiful houses on Cowey Rd.
Not only do these dilapidated properties devalue the area – they also attract the criminal element. I have someone who will go inside and shoot the vagrants and whoonga dealers who have set up shop in one of Yunus’ abandoned houses.
Many developers like Yunus argue that AMAFA make progress difficult and expensive. They say 60years is a ridiculous cut off. This means any building erected before 1955 cannot be touched without their nod of approval – and it’s costing thousands of home and business owners in Durban and the rest of KwaZulu-Natal big tom and major delays.
Applicants have to bear the cost of getting permission from neighbours or sending registered letters to neighbours. Depending on where you live, you may have to send out letters to at least eight neighbours – and possibly up to 40 neighbours if they are within a 100m radius.
SERIOUS CONSEQUENCES
Heritage legislation provided for a maximum jail term of up to five years for the most serious offenders.
EXPERT
Professor Brian Kearney, who has authored and co-authored several books, including: Architecture in Natal, 1824-1893; Traditional Hindu Temples in South Africa; Verandas in the Mist; and A Warrior’s Gateway: Durban and the Anglo-Boer War as well as a book, commissioned by the city, of revised listed important places and buildings in Durban, says they have a point.
Westville, Reservoir Hills, Durban North and Berea had many houses that were more than 50 and 60 years old. In five to 10 years, 80 percent of the houses will fall under this rule. He says many of the buildings don’t hold any architectural merit or value.
BUT he also says that people need to understand why the process was needed. “In Cape Town, for example, such a process has worked, where structures of value are protected, and modern buildings are erected behind, without hurting the valued property.”
He suggests the age be moved to 100 years.
AMAFA
Yesterday Amafa / Heritage KwaZulu Natali made an application to the city that would allow them to Durban expropriate historical properties in Durban’s Berea that have been abandoned – or intentionally left to rot so they eventually have to be demolished.
This is sure to upset developers who have taking the Trojan horse route!

Press Release:


Heritage to Decay
Durban’s Berea was once home to classic Victorian mansions, but decay is rapidly setting in and changing the face of this prized historical suburb. Residents are up in arms about several historical homes left to rot and later being demolished to make way for high-rise developments. Carte Blanche asks - is enough being done to protect Durban’s heritage?


Script:


HERITAGE WARS
VO: The Berea in Durban is a grand old suburb, with views that overlook the city.
Known for its impressive collection of classic Edwardian and Victorian houses and Art Deco buildings, this upmarket neighbourhood is much sought after.
Or at least it was.
The picture perfect suburb is being defaced by a growing number of heritage homes that have been left to rot.
Andre Nel and Trudi Low-Shang run a nursery school next door to three decaying houses on Problem Mhkize Rd.
Andre: I mean these pools when it rains...the mosquitoes. We have had to beam our properties because all the vagrants jump over the wall and they jump in here.
Derek: I mean that looks like a beautiful house, or was.
Andre: I can remember when I worked for a financial institution we did bonds on these properties and I can remember walking through them and the floors were immaculate. Absolutely stunning.

VO: These derelict houses have become such an eye sore that residents have formed an activist group called “Save Our Berea”.
Cheryl Johnson is leading the charge.
Derek: Do you think it’s all part of a plot so to speak?
Cheryl: It seems as though that the intention is to let these houses to deteriorate to a point that Amafa has no option to give them a demolition order.

VO: Amafa is the provinces heritage conservation agency. It is illegal to alter or demolish buildings more than 60-years-old without their approval

All three of the houses next door to Andre and Trudi date back to the early 1900’s, and are owned by developer Mohammed Aziz Khan who lives in this mansion, also on the Berea.

And Ros Devereaux is from Amafa.

Ros: We are not in the business of condoning demolition by neglect. So they must realise that there may be required to reinstate.

VO: Khan did not respond to numerous attempts to contact him.

Alan Ross lives in a charming Victorian House in Currie Road, two roads up from Trudi and Andre.

He is concerned that the city seems to be approving developments that will change the face of this historical suburb forever.

He bought his home 40 years ago and planned to retire here.

That’s until the heritage home next door was demolished- allegedly without Amafa’s go-ahead and this multi storey building began to take shape in its place.

Alan says a worker on site told him the plans had been drawn up overseas.

Alan: And the buildings like this were in Dubai and it was their view that Durban should become Dur-bai.
Derek: Durban should become Durbai?
Alan: Durbai.

VO: Ros is not happy.

By law the block is considered a heritage grouping.

Ros: If we had had that application for 317, then we would have considered Surrey Mansions which is one lot away from this site.

VO: Surry Mansions is a protected Art Deco building.

Derek: But how can it be approved without Amafa ?

Carte Blanche asks - is enough being done to protect Durban’s heritage? Script: HERITAGE WARS VO: The Berea in Durban is a grand old suburb, with views that overlook the city. Known for its impressive collection of classic Edwardian and Victorian houses and Art Deco buildings, this upmarket neighbourhood is much sought after. Or at least it was. The picture perfect suburb is being defaced by a growing number of heritage homes that have been left to rot. Andre Nel and Trudi Low-Shang run a nursery school next door to three decaying houses on Problem Mhkize Rd. Andre: I mean these pools when it rains...the mosquitoes. We have had to beam our properties because all the vagrants jump over the wall and they jump in here. Derek: I mean that looks like a beautiful house, or was. Andre: I can remember when I worked for a financial institution we did bonds on these properties and I can remember walking through them and the floors were immaculate. Absolutely stunning. VO: These derelict houses have become such an eye sore that residents have formed an activist group called “Save Our Berea”. Cheryl Johnson is leading the charge. Derek: Do you think it’s all part of a plot so to speak? Cheryl: It seems as though that the intention is to let these houses to deteriorate to a point that Amafa has no option to give them a demolition order. VO: Amafa is the provinces heritage conservation agency. It is illegal to alter or demolish buildings more than 60-years-old without their approval All three of the houses next door to Andre and Trudi date back to the early 1900’s, and are owned by developer Mohammed Aziz Khan who lives in this mansion, also on the Berea. And Ros Devereaux is from Amafa. Ros: We are not in the business of condoning demolition by neglect. So they must realise that there may be required to reinstate. VO: Khan did not respond to numerous attempts to contact him. Alan Ross lives in a charming Victorian House in Currie Road, two roads up from Trudi and Andre. He is concerned that the city seems to be approving developments that will change the face of this historical suburb forever. He bought his home 40 years ago and planned to retire here. That’s until the heritage home next door was demolished- allegedly without Amafa’s go-ahead and this multi storey building began to take shape in its place. Alan says a worker on site told him the plans had been drawn up overseas. Alan: And the buildings like this were in Dubai and it was their view that Durban should become Dur-bai. Derek: Durban should become Durbai? Alan: Durbai. VO: Ros is not happy. By law the block is considered a heritage grouping. Ros: If we had had that application for 317, then we would have considered Surrey Mansions which is one lot away from this site. VO: Surry Mansions is a protected Art Deco building. Derek: But how can it be approved without Amafa ? Ros: We would like to know that. LINK: This has got to be one of the best views in Durban, 180 degrees and more... we’ll that’s until 317 Currie Rd grew, and grew and grew. VO: Advocate Tayob Aboobaker lives on the other side of the development. Tayob: The people who occupy this unit will see into my bedroom, into my TV lounge. VO: The original plans were for a four storey building. Tayob: And then suddenly this plan is put in – a deviation plan. The deviation plan increased the bulk of this development by 5,400 metres VO: And the building shot up to 9 floors. Tayob: This is a whole new plan! VO: The city’s own urban plan for the Berea says properties should remain residential. Yet the city rezoned this plot to a Gr5 allowing for a commercial, high-density residential development from boundary to boundary. Alan: Which maybe should be on the beach front or the CBD. VO: In an email from their lawyer, Serengiti Properties said that they have “At all stages proceeded on the basis of lawful approvals for the rezoning of the property concerned from a GR1 to a GR5 zoning and for the approval of the relevant building plans for the building erected on the property in accordance with that zoning g". Alan alleges that residents weren’t properly notified. Only a few received a notice – and even then it didn’t say anything about a GR 5 rezoning. Aboobaker: Otherwise you are not being open or transparent and that is what the Constitution requires. VO: Alan says he had to go down to city hall to get clarity. Alan: And you have to object before the 21st May. Derek: Did you? Alan: Yes, there it is. VO: He never got a response. Cheryl says she’s not surprised. In a similar case a few blocks away, as many as 47 objections were dismissed. Cheryl: We were really shocked because it seems as though the people who made the decision in the City just ignored those objections. VO: Musa Mbhele is the new head of Development and Planning at eThekweni Municipality. Musa: When you read those you find that they talk about only three or four substantive issues really, so the number doesn’t really say that there is substance in that particular objection . VO: We wanted clarity on why the city approved the rezoning in Currie Road and passed the deviation plans. Musa: We made a decision and that decision is being challenged in court, and we are defending that particular decision. So for me to basically divulge even the so called generic information about that particular case it is a sub judice issue it will be very dangerous. VO: The residents have taken them to court, hoping to overturn the rezoning. Meanwhile, Alan says he’s had to duck building debris falling into his yard because there is virtually no space between his wall and the construction. Derek: Geez I don’t believe it, this has all fallen in the garden? Alan: Yes. Derek: This? This would flatten...feel the weight of it. VO: Serengeti denies all the allegations made against them, saying for now, they cannot comment in detail because of the pending High Court review, adding that the building "once completed, will be far more environmentally friendly and aesthetically pleasing than the surrounding buildings." Aboobaker: I say no reasonable town planner, in his right mind would ever have approved the rezoning. VO: The city’s own building bylaw says approval should not be given to developments that among other things, create a danger to life and property. The Department of Labour has therefore issued an instruction to stop building until proper safety measures are in place. VO: Cheryl is worried that the rezoning in Currie Road will set off a domino effect. Cheryl: There are developers who are acting in bad faith and it’s happening more and more. LINK: This is the other side of the story. Right in the middle of the Berea, in fact on Cowiey Road, now known as Problem Mhkize Road, and boy, are there problems. Ward councillors Martin Meyer and Jethro Lefevre say the house at 325 has been vacant for about 9 years. Martin: We are 300m away from Florida Road which for tourism is a hot spot for the city. VO: He says it can take months to get the go-ahead from Amafa for the smallest alteration. Mike: One took over seven months. I’ve now got another one, 5 months and another one, 4 months. No answer from Amafa. Ros: We need more expertise. Derek: You do? Ros: Yes, we do. Jethro: We need the municipality to take a stronger stance on derelict buildings. We have to be able to expropriate buildings in a certain time frame to stop this kind of rack and ruin coming into our neighbourhood. Owner Ismail Tayob’s lawyer says they are delaying demolition because they are waiting for a GR5 rezoning application to come through for a property across the road. “Once their rezoning is complete he (Tayob) will apply for the same zoning status. “. Derek: What can happen when a property gets into this state? Martin: The City up’s your rates, it can up it up to 15 times more the normal city rates but these developers can afford it and they pay it. Derek: Do you think anybody is paying here? Martin: The rates on this property are up to date as far as I know. Derek: Really? Martin: A new by-law has been voted on but that in not in the new by-law. That you cannot just come up with equipment and demolish somebody’s house or expropriate it willy-nilly. VO: Trudi and Andre say they are fed up. They’d rather have a shopping centre next door than the 3 unsightly decaying houses. Andre: We have parents coming to view the school to enrol their children. They walk up my stairs and the first thing they look to the left and they see this! VO: Advocate Aboobaker wants the development next door to him torn down. He points to a recent case at Kenton-on-Sea near Port Alfred. In 2012 the Supreme Court of Appeal ruled that this luxury R8 million home be demolished – 10 years after construction because it had been built without the necessary planning permits. Musa: I would assume that if we lose the case then the main respondents will have to act in accordance with what the court says. Cheryl: We welcome development but it must be within the rules. It must be within the law. They benefit from it but the people around them do not benefit from it. metadata.Summary: Architectural activists say dodgy developers are buying up protected heritage buildings in Durban, and allowing them to rot so that they can slap parking lots and high-rises in their place, changing the face of some of the city’s most historical suburbs. They alleged that city planning is helping them do it. And from the evidence this certainly seems to be the case. VISUAL TREATMENT: Seems it’s a story dealing with architecture I think it would be visually relevant to shoot interviews, links etc in “architectural settings” relevant to the subject matter. So if we are speaking to Prof Professor Brian Kearney about DBN being regarded as one of the most significant repositories of Art Deco – we could look at including an angle during the interview that would look skyward from the feet to show such a building towering behind. I have spoken to cameraman Ryan Logie (he has just bought a camera similar to the one Ian Millar used in CT to shoot the foetal surgery story – you like the images) He has a set of portable tracks we can make use off. We’ll also get some good time lapses of some of the art deco/Edwardian and Victorian buildings in Durban. These “grand design” shots will be contrasted with the derelict shots of the heritage buildings that have been left to rot and the massive concrete blocks of apartments/parking lots.
metadata.Further information: THE STORY • THE PINK HOUSE MAIN CHARACTER: Cheryl Johnson. Very articulate and passionate. A features writer for magazines. The Save our Berea is a group of architects and residents who have come together, specifically to protest against eThekwini's lack of by-law enforcement and serial neglect of a historically important buildings on Durban’s Berea. The organisation was started by Cheryl Johnson 18months ago (Her husband is a well known Durban architect) when a 100 year old tin and iron home on Essenwood Rd– known to Durbanites as “The Pink House” – was unceremoniously flattened and an a parking garage type began to be built. The home had belonged to an old lady who had passed away. (We have photos of the house before from the family) It is illegal in Durban to alter or demolish listed buildings more than 60-years-old, without approval procedures, including the need to advertise in the KZN Government Gazette and to allow for a new 30-day period for objections. The “Pink House” should have been protected building. Cheryl began investigating and discovered that AMAFA had given the new owners permission to demolish because the home had been set ablaze and virtually destroyed. If heritage buildings are deemed unsafe AMAFA will allow it to be pulled down. And here is where things start to go awry. According to the fire department it was an act of arson. They opened a case but unfortunately they couldn’t pinpoint who had set the fire. (Have copy of docket/they found an accelerant) Suspicious, she began to dig deeper. When the city refused to hand over information regarding the planning and building of the new parking lot she used PAIA and uncovered all kinds of discrepancies. • The original plans were submitted by un unregistered architect (illegal) • That the plans submitted to the city and AMAFA are different plans. • The plans submitted to AMAFA have a forged signature of another (registered) architect on them. • Apparently it’s possible to stand outside the building with the plans and point out 137 discrepancies between what’s being built and the plans at the city. Cheryl says this investigation opened a can of worms across the Berea. She started a website called “Save Our Berea” within days she had 40 000 members and at their first meeting over 400 people arrived. Here are some of the other cases: • 317 CURRIE ROAD MAIN CHARACTER: Advocate T Abubaker. Also articulate and passionate. CURRENT: This court battle starts today. Currie Road in Durban has major historical significance in Durban. Virtually every home on the road is a protected building. Many of the city’s first Indian merchants who came to trade in the 1900’s built homes along this road. They were forcibly removed later. Now there is a battle looming over a high-rise development that has been slapped adjacent on top of and adjacent to some classic Victorian styled homes. Despite the cities own plan for the area that says the properties should remain Gr1 – residential, the developers at 317 Currier Rd managed to get the city to rezone just this plot to a Gr5 - commercial, high-density, high-rise buildings. Other Concerns: • The plans originally said a 3 storey building – now it’s up to 9 floors. • The building is devaluating the properties next to it (not allowed according to building and city planning by laws – I have the legislation) • The homes around it are cast in shadow for a large portion of the day (though we could so a nice time delay) • But the residents accuse the municipality of flouting bylaws by allowing the development. The law simply states that intentions to rezone property should be advertised to everyone within 100 metres of the said property, but many say they weren’t informed. (I have a group who can confirm this) Advocate Abubaker is fuming. There is literally no more than a few inches of space between his balcony and the wall of the high-rise. He is leading the charge against the developers and the city. Other related cases: 1. Cadogan Gardens resident Hardy Wilson said he was aware of the development when he bought his flat in December 2012. “I went to the municipality to inquire about the development and they showed me approved plans for a four-storey building. The amended plans were only approved this year.” 2. One of the most affected buildings is 6 Winter Gardens, which has units valued at more than R6 million. The new development stands directly in front of it. Alan Ross, who lives next to the development, said he had received the notice for the rezoning application, but he said it was incorrectly phrased and most of the details had been omitted. Ross is concerned about his privacy and said occupants of the new building would have an unobstructed view into parts of his home. The residents said they had made numerous trips to the municipal offices, but had been denied access to building plans, officials citing “copyright reasons”. WHAT THE CITY / DEVELOPERS HAVE TO SAY eThekwini spokeswoman Tozi Mthethwa said due process had been followed and all the affected neighbours were correctly notified. She said that the municipality is unaware of any irregularities in the process and, if there were any, the affected parties should have brought the complaint to the municipality’s attention at that point, not three years later. The developer, Serengeti Rise Industries (Pty) Ltd, lawyer Richard Hoal, says that the company is constructing in accordance with an approved building plan and other approvals granted by the eThekwini Municipality. He say anything about the changing of plans from four storeys to nine storeys. • POYNTON ROAD It seems that even when people do object to a development their complaints are ignored. Another parking lot type development has been pushed through the city council despite 47 listed objections by residents. The main fellow is Wayne Webb, he is a carpenter, BUT with 4 degrees including a masters in math. He’s a bit of a hippy type, but super smart and passionate. I don’t want to clutter the story with people – so I may just get Cheryl to run through this point with us. • THE TROJAN HOUSES There are a whole bunch of beautiful homes on the Berea that are being left to rot by developers in the hopes that AMAFA will grant them demolition orders. I suggest we talk to one who has at least 2 different properties: Yunus Motalla. He’s a millionaire and can certainly afford to fix up these properties. He is the one with plans (although unconfirmed yet) to build a bottle store on top of one of the most beautiful houses on Cowey Rd. Not only do these dilapidated properties devalue the area – they also attract the criminal element. I have someone who will go inside and shoot the vagrants and whoonga dealers who have set up shop in one of Yunus’ abandoned houses. Many developers like Yunus argue that AMAFA make progress difficult and expensive. They say 60years is a ridiculous cut off. This means any building erected before 1955 cannot be touched without their nod of approval – and it’s costing thousands of home and business owners in Durban and the rest of KwaZulu-Natal big tom and major delays. Applicants have to bear the cost of getting permission from neighbours or sending registered letters to neighbours. Depending on where you live, you may have to send out letters to at least eight neighbours – and possibly up to 40 neighbours if they are within a 100m radius. SERIOUS CONSEQUENCES Heritage legislation provided for a maximum jail term of up to five years for the most serious offenders. EXPERT Professor Brian Kearney, who has authored and co-authored several books, including: Architecture in Natal, 1824-1893; Traditional Hindu Temples in South Africa; Verandas in the Mist; and A Warrior’s Gateway: Durban and the Anglo-Boer War as well as a book, commissioned by the city, of revised listed important places and buildings in Durban, says they have a point. Westville, Reservoir Hills, Durban North and Berea had many houses that were more than 50 and 60 years old. In five to 10 years, 80 percent of the houses will fall under this rule. He says many of the buildings don’t hold any architectural merit or value. BUT he also says that people need to understand why the process was needed. “In Cape Town, for example, such a process has worked, where structures of value are protected, and modern buildings are erected behind, without hurting the valued property.” He suggests the age be moved to 100 years. AMAFA Yesterday Amafa / Heritage KwaZulu Natali made an application to the city that would allow them to Durban expropriate historical properties in Durban’s Berea that have been abandoned – or intentionally left to rot so they eventually have to be demolished. This is sure to upset developers who have taking the Trojan horse route!
